rationale: While clinical literature on nonketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH) and inborn errors of metabolism establishes that an elevated CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio is the classic hallmark separating primary glycine cleavage system deficiency from secondary hyperammonemias or other non-cleavage glycine elevations, reports in multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome associated with FDXR (OMIM #620423) demonstrate that affected patients can present with simultaneous elevations in plasma glycine, CSF glycine, and an elevated glycine ratio. Consequently, a normal CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio cannot be reliably assumed to rule in or out FDXR deficiency versus attenuated forms of NKH.

evidence.text: OMIM entry 620423 documents that in multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome associated with FDXR, plasma glycine, CSF glycine, and their ratio were found to be elevated at 1 year of age.

conflicts: OMIM entry 620423 reports that in FDXR-associated multiple mitochondrial dysfunctions syndrome, the CSF-to-plasma glycine ratio itself was elevated, directly contradicting the premise that the ratio remains strictly normal in FDXR deficiency to cleanly differentiate it from primary glycine encephalopathy.

new_directions.question_text: Across all published FDXR-deficient patients with paired CSF and plasma amino acid profiles, what is the precise numerical distribution of CSF-to-plasma glycine ratios compared to classic and attenuated NKH cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Secondary lipoic acid cofactor deficiencies impair the H-protein of the glycine cleavage system, which may raise CSF glycine sufficiently to breach standard pathological ratio cutoffs (>0.08), muddying discrimination.

new_directions.question_text: Does measuring CSF serine and threonine (or the CSF serine/threonine ratio) reliably differentiate secondary glycine cleavage impairment in FDXR deficiency from primary NKH?
new_directions.rationale: Swanson et al. (2022) showed that primary NKH induces distinctive perturbations in CSF serine enantiomers and threonine; identifying whether mitochondrial Fe-S biogenesis disorders replicate this profile could provide an alternative biochemical biomarker.
